strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: reducing high-fidelity simulation budget in SBI, which is highly relevant across scientific domains with costly simulators.

The core idea—pretraining a neural density estimator on cheap low-fidelity simulations and fine-tuning via transfer learning on scarce high-fidelity simulations—is simple, intuitive, and shown to be broadly applicable.

Evaluation spans a task with an analytical ground-truth posterior (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process) plus two realistic, computationally expensive neuroscience simulators (multicompartment neuron model and a large recurrent spiking network with plasticity), lending some external validity beyond toy benchmarks.

The paper extends the method to sequential/active variants (MF-TSNPE, A-MF-TSNPE) and provides thorough algorithmic descriptions and appendix details (priors, architectures, simulator specifics) that aid reproducibility.
Ablations on the amount of low-fidelity pretraining data and on mismatched parameter dimensionality between low- and high-fidelity models provide some insight into when/why the method works.
Reports multiple diagnostic evaluations (C2ST, NLTP, posterior predictive checks, simulation-based calibration) rather than relying on a single metric.
weaknesses: No empirical comparison against existing multifidelity inference methods discussed in related work (e.g., multifidelity ABC/SMC-ABC, ROPE-style calibration), despite these being the most relevant baselines; the only compared method is vanilla (T)SNPE, which likely overstates the relative contribution.

The technical novelty is limited: the method is essentially standard transfer learning (warm-starting network weights) applied to an existing NPE pipeline, without new algorithmic or theoretical machinery for handling fidelity mismatch, parameter dimensionality mismatch, or degree of simulator misspecification.

The treatment of high-fidelity-only parameters as 'dummy variables' during low-fidelity pretraining is an ad hoc engineering choice without theoretical justification or systematic analysis of its limits (e.g., how much dimensionality mismatch can be tolerated before benefits vanish).

No theoretical or systematic empirical analysis of sensitivity to low-/high-fidelity similarity or degree of model misspecification, despite the paper explicitly acknowledging that performance depends on this similarity.

Active learning extension (A-MF-TSNPE) yields only marginal improvements over MF-TSNPE while incurring substantially higher computational cost (ensemble training) and additional hyperparameters, weakening this contribution's practical value.

Real-world tasks lack ground-truth posteriors, so claims of posterior accuracy rely on indirect proxies (NLTP, posterior predictive checks, SBC) rather than direct validation, limiting the strength of the accuracy claims.
Sample sizes for some evaluations are modest (e.g., 30 observations for the OU C2ST comparison), and variability/robustness across different low-fidelity model choices is not explored.

Efficiency claims are based solely on number of high-fidelity simulations; the added computational overhead of pretraining and network fine-tuning (and wall-clock comparisons) is not clearly quantified, which is important for an efficiency-focused method.

The discussion of related multifidelity ABC/SBI methods is thorough, but the absence of head-to-head comparisons leaves it unclear how MF-NPE's efficiency gains compare quantitatively to these alternatives.

strengths: The idea of combining transfer learning with neural posterior estimation to leverage cheap low-fidelity simulators for expensive high-fidelity simulators is a natural and practically motivated extension of SBI to a common scientific setting.

The method is evaluated on three diverse tasks spanning a tractable statistical benchmark (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck) and two genuinely expensive real-world neuroscience simulators (multicompartmental neuron model, plastic spiking network), which is a reasonable attempt at demonstrating practical relevance.
The paper includes several sensible diagnostics (C2ST against ground truth, NLTP, posterior predictive checks, simulation-based calibration) rather than relying on a single metric.
The paper is clearly related to existing multifidelity ABC/Bayesian and misspecification literature, and situates the contribution reasonably within that context.
Algorithmic descriptions (MF-NPE, MF-TSNPE, A-MF-TSNPE) are given in full pseudocode in the appendix, aiding reproducibility of the core procedure.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is essentially applying standard transfer learning (fine-tuning a pretrained network) to NPE — a well-established technique in deep learning transplanted with minimal novel adaptation; the technical novelty is thin, especially given the paper's own admission that dummy-variable handling for mismatched parameter dimensionality is a stopgap that could be improved by architectural changes not explored.

No comparison to existing multifidelity SBI/ABC baselines (e.g., Prescott & Baker multifidelity ABC, ROPE/Wehenkel et al.) is provided; the only baseline is vanilla NPE/TSNPE, which is a weak comparison given multifidelity ABC methods with likelihood-free settings already exist and are discussed in related work but never empirically benchmarked against.

The choice and quality of low-fidelity models are hand-crafted per task by domain expertise (Gaussian iid approximation, single-compartment neuron, mean-field theory) with no systematic study of how sensitive MF-NPE is to the quality/similarity of the low-fidelity model to the high-fidelity one — the discussion acknowledges this dependency but provides no empirical characterization or ablation (e.g., degrading the low-fidelity model progressively).

The acquisition-function-based A-MF-TSNPE introduces potential proposal bias without correction, and the authors admit they cannot rule out that hyperparameter tuning could change results; despite this, the reported benefit is described as "minor," undermining the contribution of the second listed core contribution (active learning schemes).

Real cost accounting is incomplete/inconsistent: the actual wall-clock cost of generating large numbers of low-fidelity simulations (e.g., 10^5) is not reported for the two real-world tasks, making the claimed "two orders of magnitude fewer high-fidelity simulations" difficult to interpret in terms of total compute savings versus NPE, since a large low-fidelity dataset also requires significant pretraining compute.

Statistical rigor is limited: no significance testing between MF-NPE and NPE curves beyond overlapping confidence intervals; sample sizes for network initializations (10) are modest given the high-dimensional flow models used.

The paper only tests one type of density estimator (neural spline flows) and one transfer-learning strategy (full fine-tuning without freezing), leaving unexplored whether the benefits are specific to this architecture or would generalize, weakening claims of general applicability.

The dimensionality of tested problems remains fairly low (up to ~24 parameters), so claims of scalability to "high-dimensional parameter spaces" typical of top-tier venues are not substantiated, and the discussion itself concedes this is an open limitation.

The improvement over NPE, while consistent, is often modest in absolute terms in several plots (e.g., C2ST differences shrink at higher HF budgets and NLTP curves converge), raising questions about the practical significance of the method outside the very low-budget regime that is emphasized.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: reducing high-fidelity simulation budget for SBI via transfer learning from low-fidelity simulators, which is timely given the growing use of SBI for costly scientific simulators.

The core idea (pretrain a neural density estimator on cheap low-fidelity simulations, fine-tune on scarce high-fidelity simulations) is simple, intuitive, and clearly presented, with a clean algorithmic description (Algorithm 1) and extensions to sequential/truncated NPE (MF-TSNPE) and an active-learning variant (A-MF-TSNPE).

Evaluation spans three diverse settings: an analytically tractable Ornstein-Uhlenbeck benchmark with known ground truth (via C2ST), and two realistic, computationally expensive neuroscience simulators (multicompartmental neuron model, recurrent spiking network with plasticity), which strengthens external validity beyond toy problems.

Demonstrates the method's applicability when low- and high-fidelity models have mismatched parameter dimensionality (via dummy variables), which is a practically relevant scenario and is explicitly tested (OU2/OU3/OU4, and the 12-vs-24-parameter spiking network task).

Reports consistent and fairly substantial efficiency gains (up to ~2 orders of magnitude fewer high-fidelity simulations) across tasks, with reasonable additional diagnostics (posterior predictive checks, simulation-based calibration) that support that the estimated posteriors are not just efficient but also reasonably well-calibrated.

Comparisons include multiple ablations of low-fidelity dataset size (10^3/10^4/10^5) showing sensible monotonic trends, and thoughtful discussion of when the acquisition-function variant helps vs. its added cost, which shows attention to nuance rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: The main baseline throughout is vanilla NPE (and its sequential variant TSNPE); there is no comparison against other multifidelity SBI baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., multifidelity ABC/SMC-ABC methods of Prescott & Baker) even in the tractable OU setting where such comparisons would be feasible, making it hard to assess whether the gains are specific to the proposed transfer-learning approach or would be matched by simpler multifidelity alternatives.

The method's real-world validation is confined to two neuroscience simulators; no experiments outside neuroscience are included despite the motivating discussion spanning aerodynamics, climate modeling, etc., which limits evidence for the claimed general applicability across scientific domains.

No systematic ablation or sensitivity analysis is provided on how the degree of low-/high-fidelity mismatch (beyond dimensionality) affects performance, despite this being flagged as a central limitation in the Discussion; a controlled experiment varying similarity between LF and HF models would strengthen the paper's claims about robustness/failure modes.

The acquisition-function-based A-MF-TSNPE shows only marginal improvement over MF-TSNPE at substantially higher computational and hyperparameter-tuning cost, and the paper acknowledges this without deeper investigation, somewhat weakening the sequential/active-learning contribution as currently presented.

Statistical rigor for the neuroscience tasks is comparatively thinner than for the OU task: NLTP is used instead of a ground-truth-based metric, and while SBC and posterior predictive checks are shown, no formal significance testing or variance analysis (beyond confidence intervals in one aggregate plot) is provided to substantiate the magnitude of claimed improvements over NPE.

The construction/choice of low-fidelity models (e.g., i.i.d. Gaussian, single-compartment neuron, partial mean-field theory) appears somewhat ad hoc/task-specific and reliant on domain expertise; the paper does not discuss how practitioners without strong domain intuition might select or construct appropriate low-fidelity approximations, which could limit reproducibility/generality of the approach in practice.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: making SBI feasible for computationally expensive simulators via multifidelity/transfer learning, with clear real-world motivation (neuroscience biophysical models, spiking networks).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across four benchmark tasks (SIR, SLCP, OU process, Gaussian Blob) and two genuinely expensive, likelihood-free neuroscience simulators (multicompartmental neuron model, plastic spiking network), covering varied properties (differing parameter dimensionality, partial observability, high-dimensional image observations).

The method is applied consistently to both amortized (NPE) and sequential/non-amortized (TSNPE) settings, and further extended with an uncertainty-based acquisition function (A-MF-TSNPE), showing a coherent family of methods rather than a single trick.

Reasonably strong and fair baselines: comparison against NPE, TSNPE, and MF-ABC, with sensitivity analysis over MF-ABC hyperparameters, and cost accounting (simulation vs. training wall-clock time) that clarifies when the multifidelity approach is actually worthwhile.

Useful exploratory analysis (Appendix B) probing when transfer/pretraining helps, using mutual information and representational coherence as explanatory factors, plus posterior-distance analyses (Appendix J) showing that similarity of LF/HF posteriors is not required for transfer to work.
Good reproducibility documentation of hyperparameters, training procedures, and task specifications; code/data promised to be released.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution (fine-tuning a pretrained density estimator on high-fidelity data) is a fairly direct application of standard transfer learning to NPE/TSNPE; the technical novelty is incremental rather than a fundamentally new inference mechanism.

The paper explicitly acknowledges several concurrent works (Thiele et al. 2025, Hikida et al. 2025, Saoulis et al. 2025) that tackle essentially the same problem of multifidelity SBI via transfer learning/distillation, yet provides no empirical or conceptual comparison to these methods, leaving the paper's relative contribution unclear.

The theoretical grounding is thin: Appendix C merely reproduces the standard NPE convergence proof (unrelated to the multifidelity aspect), and the "when does pretraining help" investigation (Sec 4.4, Appendix B) is a small, somewhat ad hoc controlled experiment rather than a rigorous characterization; the authors themselves state that no theoretical guarantees are provided.

A-MF-TSNPE, the more sophisticated active-learning variant, shows only marginal or inconsistent gains over MF-TSNPE in several tasks (e.g., SLCP, SIR) while incurring substantially higher computational overhead (ensemble training), limiting its practical value.

The low-fidelity simulator cost is assumed negligible throughout the main experiments, which is a significant simplification; the important question of optimal budget allocation between fidelities is deferred entirely to future work.

Benchmark tasks with articifically constructed low-fidelity models (e.g., OU-process with i.i.d. Gaussian LF model) may not fully represent real scientific use cases where LF/HF relationships are less controllable, and the choice of LF models across tasks appears to be hand-designed by the authors, raising some concern about generalizability of the reported gains.

Much of the essential methodological/empirical detail (algorithms, cost breakdowns, calibration checks, multi-fidelity extension) is relegated to a very large appendix, suggesting the main paper alone may not fully substantiate all claims without extensive supplementary reading.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: reducing the number of expensive high-fidelity simulations needed for simulation-based inference.

The proposed method (transfer-learning-based pretraining on a low-fidelity simulator, followed by fine-tuning on high-fidelity data) is simple, easy to implement, and compatible with existing NPE/TSNPE pipelines.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation spanning four benchmark tasks (SIR, SLCP, OU process, Gaussian Blob) and two genuinely expensive, realistic neuroscience simulators (multicompartment neuron model, plastic spiking network), which is more application diversity than typical SBI method papers.

Includes ablations examining when transfer learning helps (mismatched parameter dimensionality, mutual information/representational coherence experiments), simulation-based calibration checks, and cost-accounting appendices (simulation vs. training time).
Reasonably thorough documentation of tasks, priors, hyperparameters, and algorithms in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core contribution is essentially standard fine-tuning transfer learning applied to an existing method (TSNPE), plus an already-known ensemble-variance acquisition function (Lueckmann et al. 2019); the combination, while reasonable, is incremental rather than a substantive algorithmic advance.

No empirical comparison to the concurrent (but directly relevant) multifidelity SBI methods explicitly cited (Thiele et al. 2025, Hikida et al. 2025, Saoulis et al. 2025); even as 'concurrent' work, some empirical positioning relative to these would substantially strengthen claims of state-of-the-art efficiency.

The comparison to MF-ABC, used to argue large efficiency gains, is explicitly acknowledged as potentially unfair due to limited hyperparameter tuning of the baseline, undermining the strength of one of the paper's central efficiency claims.

A-MF-TSNPE, the more sophisticated active-learning variant, shows inconsistent benefits (improves on OU but not SLCP/SIR), and its added ensemble training cost is only justified in narrow settings—this weakens the practical value of the proposed acquisition-based extension.

The 'when does pretraining help' analysis (mutual information/representational coherence) is confined to a small synthetic OU2 perturbation study and does not provide a general, actionable framework or theory; the convergence proof in Appendix C is a standard/trivial NPE consistency result offering little new insight.

The abstract's headline claim of 'up to two orders of magnitude fewer simulations' is drawn from specific favorable configurations (e.g., spiking network with near-zero-cost mean-field low-fidelity model) rather than a consistent effect across tasks, giving an overstated impression of general applicability.

Total simulation-cost accounting (simulation vs. training tradeoff) is only reported for 2 of 6 tasks; for the four benchmark tasks, the paper explicitly defers this analysis, leaving the practical utility (net wall-clock savings) partially unsubstantiated.

The choice and design of low-fidelity simulators across tasks appear heavily hand-crafted with domain expertise per-task, raising concerns about generalizability of the approach to settings without an obvious/cheap low-fidelity counterpart, and the paper does not provide general guidance for constructing such simulators.
Real-world task evaluations rely on NLTP/NRMSE without ground-truth posteriors, limiting the strength of correctness claims relative to benchmark tasks with known reference posteriors.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: reducing the number of expensive high-fidelity simulations required for simulation-based inference by leveraging cheap low-fidelity simulators via transfer learning.

The proposed approach (MF-(TS)NPE and its sequential/active variants) is simple, general, and easy to implement on top of existing NPE/TSNPE pipelines, requiring no additional hyperparameter tuning compared to standard NPE.

Extensive empirical evaluation across four benchmark tasks (SIR, SLCP, OU process, Gaussian Blob) and two computationally expensive, realistic neuroscience simulators (multicompartmental neuron model, recurrent spiking network with plasticity), covering diverse data modalities (time series, images, spike counts) and different levels of parameter overlap between fidelities.

Consistent and often substantial simulation-efficiency gains (up to orders of magnitude fewer high-fidelity simulations) over strong baselines (NPE, TSNPE, MF-ABC), with comparable inference accuracy, and included cost analyses (Appendix K) showing when the multifidelity approach yields net wall-clock savings.

Good methodological rigor: proof of convergence of the NPE loss, validation with multiple metrics (C2ST, MMD, NLTP, NRMSE), simulation-based calibration checks, and thoughtful ablations (e.g., pretraining on joint vs. low-fidelity-only data, varying LF/HF parameter overlap, MF-ABC hyperparameter sensitivity).

The exploratory analysis of *when* pretraining helps (mutual information and representational coherence) is a nice attempt to move beyond purely empirical demonstration toward understanding the mechanism, even though it stops short of formal theory.

Reasonably thorough related work discussion situating the paper among concurrent multifidelity SBI efforts (Thiele et al., Hikida et al., Saoulis et al.) and other simulation-efficient SBI approaches, clarifying the specific niche (assumes an existing hand-crafted low-fidelity simulator plus transfer/active learning).
weaknesses: No formal theoretical analysis of when/why transfer learning should help beyond the trivial convergence proof for standard NPE (which does not involve the multifidelity aspect); the "when does pretraining help" investigation (Sec 4.4/App B) is a single small controlled experiment (OU2 with additive noise/inversion) and its generalizability to the more complex benchmark and neuroscience tasks is not established.

The method assumes a hand-crafted, domain-expert-designed low-fidelity simulator is available and cheap; this is a fairly strong assumption that limits general applicability, and the paper does not explore how sensitive performance is to poor choices of low-fidelity simulator (beyond one qualitative illustration in App J showing distance between posteriors is not predictive of transfer success).

Simulation cost accounting is incomplete: for the four main benchmark tasks (Sec 4.1) the paper explicitly does not report total (LF+HF) simulation cost, deferring this analysis only to the two neuroscience tasks; this makes it harder to assess whether the reported "orders of magnitude" HF savings translate into genuine end-to-end compute savings across all tasks, especially since LF simulation budgets used for pretraining (up to 10^5) are not free.

A-MF-TSNPE, the more sophisticated active-learning variant, shows inconsistent benefits (helps on OU process but not SLCP/SIR) and incurs substantial extra ensemble-training overhead, somewhat undercutting the contribution's practical value; the paper's own limitations section concedes this trade-off is only favorable in narrow settings.

MF-ABC baseline comparison may be somewhat unfair, as the authors acknowledge more extensive hyperparameter tuning could improve its performance, weakening the strength of the comparative claims against ABC-based multifidelity methods.

Comparisons to the concurrent multifidelity SBI works mentioned (Thiele et al. 2025, Hikida et al. 2025, Saoulis et al. 2025) are only discussed narratively, with no empirical comparison, leaving open how MF-(TS)NPE stands relative to these alternative recent multifidelity SBI paradigms.

Reproducibility relies on promised future code release rather than an anonymized repository at submission time, and some experimental design choices (e.g., choice of acquisition function, ensemble size, pretraining strategy) are only lightly justified relative to alternatives explored only briefly in the appendix.

The evaluation of transfer learning benefit versus low-fidelity model dimensionality/parameter mismatch (Sec 4.1, OU process, App E.3) shows performance degradation when parameter spaces differ substantially, but this important limitation is not deeply investigated across other tasks (e.g., SLCP with differing dimensionality is used, but not comprehensively probed for degradation patterns).
